target: Agent 1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would give everyone time to vote by removing scheduling barriers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time off, so many low-income hourly workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs would still be scheduled to work and would face the same choice between voting and earning wages.

target: Agent 2’s objection that private employers would still keep low-income workers on the job, so the holiday would not help.
objection: Even if some private workplaces remain open, a national holiday would still reduce scheduling barriers because many employers use altered holiday schedules or shorter hours, and the holiday also affects school and caregiving routines, creating a more workable voting window for working parents and hourly workers.

target: Agent 1’s claim that holiday status would reliably create a non-work window and that schools/childcare would be closed.
objection: Federal holiday status does not legally require private employers to stop operating or guarantee childcare or school-related closures, so the supposed time window for low-income workers and parents is not dependable.

target: Agent 2’s claim that employers will not be motivated to accommodate voting time just because Election Day is a holiday.
objection: Labeling Election Day a national holiday changes its social priority and creates incentives for employers to accommodate voting through holiday schedules, shift swaps, and flexible arrangements, especially in hourly customer-facing workplaces.

target: Agent 1’s claim that the holiday would create strong employer incentives to accommodate low-income workers.
objection: A holiday label does not compel private employers to close or provide paid time off, and in customer-facing sectors the costs of closing or reducing staffing remain, so the ‘celebration’ frame does not reliably produce the accommodations the argument assumes; shift-swapping also is not dependable for workers with little bargaining power.

target: Agent 2’s claim that OECD election holidays do not show a holiday would work in the United States.
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that placing elections on non-working days is a common, workable model that gives hourly and lower-income voters a realistic opportunity to vote.

target: Agent 1’s inference from OECD weekend/holiday elections to the effectiveness of an election-day holiday by itself.
objection: Those countries usually combine the holiday or weekend election with other reforms such as early voting, absentee/mail voting, or extended hours, so the holiday alone is not what solves the access problem.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a national holiday would not reliably create workplace accommodations for low-income workers.
objection: Broad bipartisan support makes it more likely that a holiday would be implemented with practical workplace accommodations, so low-income workers would more likely get an actual off-work window to vote.

target: Agent 1’s claim that bipartisan support implies enforceable or widely adopted workplace accommodations.
objection: Bipartisan support does not create a legal requirement for private employers to give paid time off or stop scheduling workers, so the holiday can remain largely symbolic for low-income workers unless paired with a specific mandate.

target: Agent 2’s claim that employers will not actually adjust schedules enough for low-income workers to vote.
objection: A national holiday changes the nation’s priority for the day, which reshapes workplace and family routines so employers and shift scheduling practices are more likely to adapt and create a workable voting window.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that employers will automatically adjust schedules because the day is nationally celebrated.
objection: The expectation of workplace adjustment is not enforceable, private employers can stay open, and workers with the least bargaining power are least likely to secure a usable window through voluntary shift swaps or informal flexibility.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday is a better turnout strategy than state-level voting reforms.
objection: Research shows an election holiday by itself does not reliably increase turnout compared with other access reforms, while state policies like employer time-off laws and automatic voter registration directly remove barriers that suppress participation.

target: Agent 2’s claim that holiday status is comparatively ineffective at increasing turnout.
objection: The main barrier is timing: work, school, and caregiving routines. A national holiday directly changes when those obligations fall, creating a realistic opportunity to vote that uneven state reforms do not provide.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that a federal holiday would create immediate, universal off-work and off-school conditions for low-income workers.
objection: Federal holiday status does not require private employers to close or provide paid leave, and many low-wage sectors keep operating; school and childcare changes are also inconsistent, so the schedule relief is not universal.

target: Agent 2’s claim that election holiday reforms are less effective than targeted administrative reforms.
objection: Automatic voter registration only reduces enrollment friction and does not solve the problem of being unable to vote during the relevant time window, whereas a holiday directly relieves the weekday scheduling barrier that blocks many low-income voters.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that moving Election Day off a weekday reliably creates a practical voting window for low-income workers.
objection: A holiday label does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many hourly workers would still be scheduled and still face the same work-versus-voting conflict despite the calendar change.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday is comparatively ineffective because it only addresses scheduling.
objection: A holiday also changes how voting is perceived, making it a shared civic event rather than an individual chore, which reduces motivational and social frictions and can encourage broader participation in addition to schedule relief.

target: Agent 1’s claim that social-motivation effects can raise turnout even if schedules remain constraining.
objection: If low-income workers still lack actual time off because employers can keep them scheduled, then a holiday’s symbolic effect does not solve the decisive barrier; motivation alone is not enough without a dependable voting window.

target: Agent 2’s reliance on automatic voter registration and similar reforms as substitutes for a holiday.
objection: Automatic voter registration may reduce enrollment friction, but it does not create time to vote; the main bottleneck for many low-income workers is weekday schedule availability, so a holiday still targets a distinct barrier those reforms leave untouched.

target: Agent 1’s claim that state-level reforms cannot replace a national holiday’s scheduling relief.
objection: State laws requiring employers to provide time off or job-protected voting leave directly address the work-related scheduling barrier, so the holiday is not uniquely necessary to solve the timing problem.

target: Agent 2’s claim that a holiday still leaves workers needing individualized permission from employers.
objection: A national holiday shifts baseline expectations so workers are less dependent on individual supervisor approval, because holiday scheduling norms and shift-swaps make it easier to take a workable voting window without having to negotiate permission one person at a time.

target: Agent 1’s claim that a holiday reduces individualized permission barriers for voting.
objection: Even on a federal holiday, private employers can remain open and schedule staff, so workers still often need supervisor approval or must absorb lost wages or shifts; the holiday does not remove the need for permission in many workplaces.

target: Agent 2’s assumption that only the worker’s own schedule matters.
objection: Low-income voters often depend on family members, rides, and childcare that are also tied to weekday work and school schedules, so a national holiday can coordinate the broader support network needed to get to the polls and be cared for while voting.

target: Agent 2’s claim that Election Day should not be a national holiday because the day would mostly be symbolic and not solve schedule pressure.
objection: The largest practical barrier to voting is the conflict with work, school, and caregiving routines; making Election Day a national holiday directly shifts those constraints at the population level, and broad bipartisan support plus OECD precedent show it is a feasible and meaningful scheduling reform.
